report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is well supported, provided “high viral load” means HBV DNA **≥200,000 IU/mL** and infants receive standard immunoprophylaxis (timely hepatitis-B vaccine, often plus HBIG). Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), begun late in pregnancy—traditionally 28–32 weeks—lowers maternal HBV DNA before delivery and reduces the residual transmission that can occur despite infant prophylaxis.

The key direct evidence is a randomized trial of highly viremic mothers: by delivery, 68% receiving TDF versus 2% of untreated controls had HBV DNA below 200,000 IU/mL; reported infant transmission was lower with TDF (5% vs 18%). This supports a clinically important effect, though the trial setting and use of infant HBIG matter. [http://www.corevih-bretagne.fr/ckfinder/userfiles/files/Congrès/CROI_2017/Articles_Mercredi_15/Pan+et+al_+-+2016+-+Tenofovir+to+Prevent+Hepatitis+B+Transmission+in+M.pdf](http://www.corevih-bretagne.fr/ckfinder/userfiles/files/Congrès/CROI_2017/Articles_Mercredi_15/Pan+et+al_+-+2016+-+Tenofovir+to+Prevent+Hepatitis+B+Transmission+in+M.pdf)

Evidence has continued to develop, including a randomized trial published in *JAMA* in 2025. [https://scholar.xjtu.edu.cn/en/publications/tenofovir-and-hepatitis-b-virus-transmission-during-pregnancy-a-r/](https://scholar.xjtu.edu.cn/en/publications/tenofovir-and-hepatitis-b-virus-transmission-during-pregnancy-a-r/)

This is reflected in WHO guidance: TDF prophylaxis is recommended for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL (or positive HBeAg where DNA testing is unavailable), preferably from the second trimester through delivery or completion of infant vaccination. [https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/186d4f3b-6f77-42d1-9392-efa6269ab7e8/content](https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/186d4f3b-6f77-42d1-9392-efa6269ab7e8/content)

TDF is prevention for transmission, not a substitute for neonatal vaccination/HBIG or maternal follow-up, including monitoring for post-treatment hepatitis flares.
